system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.
runtime: Anthropic API, effort medium, no seed or temperature, so runs do not repeat exactly

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a large consumer build-out yet. Treat the home segment as a tested option: run the proposed X1 test on compact commercial-derived home machines before any prototype investment. Keep the commercial business as the core.

frame.objective: Decide whether Simonelli Group should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (for example home espresso), beyond its existing professional espresso-equipment business, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. Be honest about how far the company already reaches individual buyers, which I have not yet verified.
constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions.
Company financial data may not be fully public; state what could not be found.
Test budget of EUR 20,000 and a 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures.
Eight searches in total, so evidence gathering must be targeted.
Must not treat a company's own claims as proof of consumer demand.
alternatives: No expansion: keep focus on commercial café and foodservice equipment, treat consumer sales as incidental.
Product redesign for home use: compact, lower-cost or prosumer machine or grinder under an existing brand.
Different route to buyers: retailers, marketplaces, direct-to-consumer, or cafés selling home-use kit.
Different customer group: home baristas or small-office users, possibly via a sub-brand.
Service and consumables model: recurring revenue from maintenance, parts, training for cafés and home users.
Brand licensing: license Victoria Arduino or Nuova Simonelli name for consumer appliances made by a partner, low capital at risk.

T1.claim: Home and prosumer espresso buyers want professional-grade components in a smaller, cheaper machine. A maker that already has commercial-grade boilers, pumps and grinders can sell a compact version at a premium over mass-market appliances, because buyers pay for the perceived quality of the parts.
T1.who_benefits: Simonelli Group (Nuova Simonelli and Victoria Arduino), which already makes the components and can reuse them, and home enthusiasts who want café-grade extraction.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who have tasted specialty coffee and know the difference between a commercial and a domestic machine trade up to a product that signals professional quality, especially when it is marketed as a prosumer machine rather than a kitchen appliance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli sells the machine or grinder at a price above mass-market home appliances, through existing dealer and online channels, using the commercial brand as the premium signal. It keeps the margin because the parts are already in-house.
assumptions: A meaningful share of home espresso buyers pay a premium for commercial-derived components.
Compact versions can be built at a cost that keeps margin above consumer-appliance levels.
Existing brand awareness with specialist buyers transfers to the consumer line.
Dealer or online channels can reach home buyers without a large new sales organisation.
predictions: Buyers in a conjoint or price test will rate a commercial-derived compact machine above a same-price mass-market rival on build quality.
Specialist retailers that stock Simonelli or Victoria Arduino commercial kit will report unprompted requests for home versions.
Sales of prosumer models will track the specialty-coffee trade-up cycle rather than general appliance demand.
A price test at 1.5x to 2x mainstream home machines will still show purchase intent above a set threshold.
T1.first_claim: Home and prosumer espresso buyers want professional-grade components in a smaller, cheaper machine. A maker that already has commercial-grade boilers, pumps and grinders can sell a compact version at a premium over mass-market appliances, because buyers pay for the perceived quality of the parts.

T2.claim: Individual buyers are not blocked by product quality. They are blocked by reach. Home espresso customers buy through retailers and consumer brands that own the shopper relationship, so a component maker gains more by supplying or licensing to those brands than by building its own consumer sales route.
T2.who_benefits: Established consumer appliance brands and retailers that already own home shoppers, plus Simonelli as a component or licence supplier earning fees or supply margin without marketing or retail costs.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Home buyers choose a machine through the brand and store they already trust and the reviews they read there. A commercial-grade name without retail presence does not change that choice, so the buying decision moves to whoever owns the retail touchpoint.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli captures value through component supply contracts, licence royalties or co-branded products made to its specification. It avoids retail, marketing and returns costs, and its margin depends on the partner's volume rather than its own consumer reach.
assumptions: Consumer appliance brands would pay for a commercial-derived component or a licensed name.
Simonelli's brand adds enough signal that a partner can charge a premium.
Partners will accept Simonelli's technical specification and quality control.
Partner sales volume exceeds what Simonelli could reach itself within the test period.
predictions: Consumer appliance brands approached with a component or licence offer will show interest, but will set terms that give Simonelli a small share of retail margin.
Home purchase decisions in surveys will rank retailer or brand trust above the commercial-brand name.
Simonelli's own direct-to-consumer trial will have higher acquisition cost per sale than a partner-channel trial.
Revenue from a partner route will be small relative to the commercial business unless the partner has large home distribution.

Home espresso customers buy through retailers and consumer brands that own the shopper relationship, so a component maker gains more by supplying or licensing to those brands than by building its own consumer sales route.

assessments.quote: Nuova Simonelli has unveiled the Oscar Mood, a colorful new model in its most affordable machine line for homes, offices and other lower-volume environments.
assessments.does_not_show: This is a trade-press account of a product launch, drawing on the company's own description. It shows that Simonelli already sells a home-oriented machine, not that home buyers pay a premium for commercial-derived components, what volumes sell, or whether buyers rate it above rival machines at the same price.

assessments.quote: has announced plans to acquire Italian prosumer espresso equipment company Lelit
assessments.does_not_show: This is an announced acquisition, not a completed one. It shows that a large consumer appliance group chose to buy an Italian prosumer espresso maker outright. It does not show that Breville would have licensed or sourced components instead, what the deal means for unit margin, or whether a component supplier would earn meaningful consumer revenue. It points toward owning a consumer-facing brand, which fits option H more than the licence route T2 predicts, so its support for T2 is weak.

assessments.quote: The approximately $3,900 machine (United States market) represents the smallest and least expensive machine in the growing La Marzocco Home espresso machine line.
assessments.does_not_show: This is a rival's launch, not a test of T1. It shows that another commercial espresso maker sees a home segment worth a dedicated machine at about $3,900 in the US, so the premium segment is real and contested. It does not show whether buyers pay for commercial-derived parts, what share or margin La Marzocco earns, or whether Simonelli would win sales. It is a challenge that raised competition, not one that disproved T1.

X1.name: Compact home machine demand and partner-channel test (proposed design)
X1.method: Two-arm, staged test. Arm A (T1, direct): a landing page and refundable pre-order for a compact, commercial-derived home machine concept, with a clear build-quality message, shown at three price points (about 1.5x, 2x and 2.5x a mainstream home machine, proposed). Arm B (T2, partner): structured interviews and a licence or component term sheet with 6-8 appliance brands or specialist retailers, asking what share of margin they would give up for the Simonelli or Victoria Arduino name. Plus a conjoint survey of home buyers rating build quality against retailer and brand trust.
X1.sample: Arm A: about 3,000 qualified home-espresso visitors reached through specialist coffee-enthusiast channels (proposed). Arm B: 6-8 consumer appliance brands and specialist retailers (proposed). Survey: about 400 home espresso buyers who bought a machine in the past 2 years (proposed).
X1.measure: Arm A: refundable deposit rate at each price point. Arm B: number of partners willing to sign a term sheet or pilot, and the margin share they would require. Survey: relative importance of commercial-component signal vs retailer/brand trust in purchase choice.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Deposit rate at the 2x price point is high enough to justify prototype development, and the conjoint shows commercial-component signal ranks above a same-price mainstream rival.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Partners sign pilots but demand most of the retail margin, and the survey ranks retailer or brand trust above the commercial-brand signal, so Simonelli's own direct route performs worse than a partner route.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to prototype under T1 only if at least 3% of Arm A visitors place a refundable deposit at the 2x price point (proposed threshold) and the conjoint shows commercial-component signal in the top two of five attributes for at least 40% of respondents (proposed). If fewer than 1 partner signs a pilot in Arm B and the survey ranks brand trust first, treat T2 as the stronger route and pursue licensing or component supply only. Otherwise do not invest; keep consumer activity incidental (option A).

revisions.reason: The simulated warehouse result is about a label printer and measured nothing about buyers or home espresso, so it changes nothing. T1 rests on the real Oscar Mood launch material and the Linea Micra challenge, which show the segment exists but not that buyers pay for commercial-derived parts. Still untested.

The simulated label-printer result (SYN-D) measured nothing about buyers or partners, so it changes nothing for T2. T2 stays uncertain. The Breville-Lelit announcement shows a consumer group buying a prosumer brand outright, which fits the ownership route (option H) better than the licence route, so it is weak support for T2 and not a reason to revise it.

What-if only: if SYN-D were real, it would show a label printer reducing packing errors in a warehouse. That bears on no buyer, wearer or home-espresso question, so T1 would be unchanged. This is a simulated result and is not evidence for T1.

final.recommendation: Do not commit a large consumer build-out yet. Simonelli already reaches some home buyers (Nuova Simonelli Oscar Mood; Victoria Arduino Eagle One Prima, a domestic machine), so the real question is whether to scale a compact commercial-derived home line. Test first with the proposed X1 test (about EUR 18,000, 10 weeks, both estimates). Keep commercial foodservice as the core and treat consumer sales as incidental until X1 reads out.
final.target_customer: Home espresso enthusiasts and prosumers who want café-grade extraction in a compact machine or grinder. A hypothesis; I found no evidence of its size.
final.value_proposition: A compact home machine or grinder built on existing commercial-grade components, priced above mainstream home appliances, using the commercial brand as the quality signal.
final.next_action: Run X1: landing-page pre-order at three price points, partner interviews for the T2 route, and a conjoint survey. Proceed to prototype only if at least 3% of visitors place a refundable deposit at the 2x price point and commercial-component signal ranks in the top two attributes for at least 40% of respondents (proposed thresholds).
final.uncertainty: High. No consumer sales volumes, margins or financials found; company financials were not publicly available to me. Evidence read is mostly company or trade-press launch material, not demand data. No independent study of whether buyers pay for commercial-derived components. Home segment is contested (La Marzocco Linea Micra, about $3,900 US). Breville-Lelit was an announced deal, completion unverified. The 2021 product plan is an Italian company claim, delivery unconfirmed. Simulated result SYN-D is irrelevant and not cited.
would_change_if: X1 deposits below 3% at 2x price, or commercial-component signal outside top two attributes: weakens T1, points to no expansion.
Partners sign pilots readily and accept most retail margin: makes T2 (licence or component supply) stronger.
Disclosed data show consumer lines already profitable at scale: supports a home sub-brand.
Independent evidence shows buyers rate commercial-derived parts no higher than mainstream parts at the same price.
Financials show margin or capacity cannot support a lower-margin consumer product.
